News.title: At least 11 killed and dozens injured as tourist bus flips after skidding off road in Mexico
News.content:
BUS SMASH At least 11 killed and dozens injured as tourist bus flips after skidding off road in Mexico

A SHOCKING tourist bus crash in Mexico has left at least 11 people dead and dozens more injured after the vehicle veered off a road.

The bus was travelling from the state of Jalisco at the time of the tragic accident.





Authorities say the bus veered off the highway and flipped over near the town of Amatlan de Canas.

The horrific crash has claimed at least 11 lives, while 31 others were injured on Friday.

Six of the victims died at the scene of the crash, according to Patrika.

The injured passengers – some of whom were in a serious condition – have all been transported to nearby hospitals for treatment.

The passengers had been en route to the recreational centre in Nayarit, according to officials.

Emergency crews from Nayarit and Jalisco rushed to the fatal scene.

The road was closed off to traffic as the rescue operations began.

An investigation has been launched into the cause of the accident.



Preliminary reports suggest that the high speed, poor road conditions and driver fatigue were potential factors.

In photos shared by the Nayarit government, the bus can be seen lying on its side and covered in mud.

Governor Pablo Lemus has since confirmed the state will cover medical and funeral costs of the victims.

On Friday, he expressed his own grief and offered his condolences to the victims’ families.

Road accidents are common in Mexico and Latin America and often are caused by a disregard for traffic regulations and road safety standards.

News.title: Two tourists die after plunging from balcony at same airport within hours in front of horrified passengers
News.content:
AIRPORT HORROR Two tourists die after plunging from balcony at same airport within hours in front of horrified passengers

TWO tourists have died after plunging from a balcony in front of horrified passengers at the same airport just hours apart.

A Chinese woman, aged 27, and an Algerian man, aged 30, both fell to their deaths at a Malaysian airport on Friday.





Both cases, which took place just hours apart are believed to be unrelated, local police said.

Chilling footage showed the 27-year-old woman sitting on a ledge in front of terrified bystanders moments before plummeting off of a balcony.

She is understood to have fallen at around 2:20pm on May 1 – with local authorities saying she had been “crying and screaming aggressively” just before her death.

Security personnel and Kuala Lumpur International staff attempted to calm the woman.

She was later taken to Putrajaya Hospital for further treatment but was tragically pronounced dead at 5:09pm local time.

Cops revealed she had been scheduled to board a return flight to China on May 1.



An investigation into her death is ongoing, police say.

Just hours after her death, at around 9:10pm, a 30-year-old Algerian man jumped from the outer balcony area on the third floor of Terminal 2.

Police said he jumped in a suspected suicide attempt.

A witness reportedly saw the man open his backpack before running towards a barrier and jumping over it.

Emergency services found him at the scene before taking him to Cyberjaya Hospital for further care.



He also died hours later at 2:55am on May 2 after succumbing to his injuries.

Local police urged the public not to speculate on either incident.

News.title: How Putin’s forces are luring kids to their deaths with ‘gingerbread’ MINES dropped from sky to wipe out Ukraine cities
News.content:
CHILDREN are being lured to their deaths by toy-like mines deployed by Russia to “depopulate” southern Ukraine.

Named “Pryanik” – Russian for “gingerbread” – they are small enough to fit in a person’s palm, round and deceptively harmless at a glance.





Yuriy Boychenko, founder of Hope For Ukraine, told The Sun that Kherson has been transformed into a de-facto urban “minefield” as Russia has been using cheap, agile FPV drones to scatter the camouflaged munitions.

This tactic is a relatively recent evolution of Russia‘s drone terror, noticed for the first time about a month ago.

Boychenko described this as the “deliberate weaponisation of backyards and doorsteps, a calculated attempt to make life uninhabitable.”

The “gingerbreads” are not designed to destroy an armoured vehicle, like a tank. Instead, they are build to maim or kill.



“Walking to a pharmacy is becoming a gamble with mutilation,” he said. “It is a big problem.

“Russia is using FPV drones to drop these mines all over residential areas in Kherson.

“If an adult steps on it, or a child finds it while playing in the grass … it will blow them up, or wound them badly.”

He added: “Right now, there are two types of dangers that civilians face – one is from the air, the FPV drones that target the directly.



“The other is the minefield underneath their feet.”

Located by the Black Sea, Kherson is almost directly on the frontline, with Russian forces lying in wait across the Dnipro River for one wrong move.

Its streets are draped in anti-drone nets, installed after Russia’s infamous “human safari,” beginning in May 2024, in the city they once occupied.



The liberation marked the beginning of a new phase of the enemy’s terror campaign, as Russian drone operators hunted Ukrainians in the streets, in real-time.

Daily life for the 60,000 residents is lived in basements. Anyone daring to step outside risks being targeted by Russian drones – and now stepping on a mine.

Stationed a mile away, Russians do not need sophisticated equipment to target residents.

“They are using first-person drones that cost as little as $500, not pricey long-range ones,” Boychenko said about the strategy.

“The Ukrainian authorities tried to put nets around the streets to prevent the mining but they cannot net the entire city.



“It is open-air terror and their goal is to make Kherson uninhabitable; to make life so miserable that people are forced to leave.

“Then, it is going to be much easier for them to re-occupy the city … we are already under 24/7 assault.

“The worst part is that residents are forced to spend most their time in basements. There is always something hanging in the air.”

Drones, as well as the mines, have made Hope for Ukraine‘s humanitarian operations near impossible.

When teams try to bring in food to desperate people, they themselves become a magnet for attacks “in a matter of minutes”.



Boychenko explained how the NGO – the only one still operating in the city – is having to adapt.

“A lot of people are hesitant to get out of their hideouts when we bring out aid,” he said.

“Every time they open the door, they listen for the high-pitched buzzing sound in the air.



“When we do distributions, we always try to find big trees [to hide under] … in open air you become a target in the matter of minutes.

“When we make deliveries, we try to schedule them during bad weather as it is much safer.”

It was only a couple of weeks ago that a Ukrainian man fell victim to one of the lethal “gingerbreads” while on a morning drive.

In January, another resident was killed instantly after stepping on a Soviet “petal” mine, deliberately scattered by Russians.

Hope for Ukraine is working to raise as much awareness about the tactic to minimise the deaths of innocents.



“Gingerbread” munitions are 3D-printed anti-personnel mines wrapped in camouflage fabric.

Their compact size make them remarkably hard to spot, as they vanish in grass and litter – sometimes even mistaken for toys.

Volodymyr Prepepelytsia, from the National Police in Kherson region, told Suspline that they are an upgraded version of the “Pryanyk” mines – but are more sophisticated and more powerful.



They appear to be a response to a shortage of standard PFM-1 “Butterfly” mines, which look like toys, making them particularly dangerous to curious children.

After testing the “gingerbread”, Perepelytsia said the average activation pressure is seven kilograms, meaning that even a toddler can trigger the explosive.

They are also prone to spontaneous self-detonation due to movement nearby.

A critical shortage of de-miners and equipment has made it difficult to clear Kherson from such highly-volatile munitions.

Teams – already under strain by larger explosives lodged in the ground – have been stretched. By no means, their efforts could match the speed of Russian forces.



As of 1 April 2026, a total of 1,431 people, including 147 children, have been injured by Russian mines and explosive remnants of war since the start of the full-scale invasion.

Russian troops ‘shooting down their OWN drones' HOPELESS Russian soldiers are reportedly shooting down their own drones and then disguising them as Ukrainian aircraft so they can claim battle bonuses. It comes as horror claims emerge that Vladimir Putin’s soldiers are turning to cannibalism as they run low on provisions. Russians have shot down their own drones due to coordination failures and administrative confusion, United24 Media reported. But Mad Vlad’s desperate lads are then pretending to have taken down Ukrainian drones so that they can claim cash rewards. Pro-Russian media describe the situation as a “time bomb”, fearing that nearly all of Putin’s drones could soon come under attack from his own hapless soldiers. The chaos is reportedly caused by drone operators not warning firing teams about their launches. And firing squads are struggling to tell Russian and Ukrainian drones apart, with one source saying: “They’ll shoot down everything they see.”

In the region of Kherson, authorities have opened 356 criminal cases of civilian casualties from mines and other explosive devices.

An estimated 140 people have been killed and 253 others wounded in the past four years.

Following in the footsteps of Princess Diana, Prince Harry has partnered with the HALO Trust to raise awareness about the importance of de-mining in Ukraine.

Strapped in body armour, the Duke of Sussex was pictured in the town of Bucha, an hour away from Kyiv – an area littered with explosives in the first few months of the war.

Speaking on the technology used by the charity, he said: “Nearly 30 years ago, when my mother visited Angola, de-miners carried out their work on their hands and knees, painstakingly uncovering hidden explosives.

“Today, thanks to innovation, they are using drones, AI and robots to do this vital work with greater precision and protection.”

News.title: Furious residents accuse Labour of ‘taking voters for fools’ with ‘miracle’ bin strike fix just days before election
News.content:
LOAD OF RUBBISH Furious residents accuse Labour of ‘taking voters for fools’ with ‘miracle’ bin strike fix just days before election

LABOUR has been accused of “taking people for fools” after suddenly announcing that an end to Birmingham’s bin strike is in sight.

After turning a blind eye to stinking rubbish heaps, disgruntled residents and rat infestations for months, Labour suddenly have a plan to fix it.





But the timing has raised eyebrows and questions, with local elections in Birmingham lurking just around the corner.

Monica McNicholas, 69, an exam invigilator, has had mountains of rubbish piling up at either end of her road in Small Heath for months.

Now, they’ve suddenly vanished.

“It’s all very convenient, them saying that there’s an end in sight just when they want our votes,” she said, adding that the street had also been given some much-needed TLC.





Earlier this week, Labour leader of the city council, John Cotton, announced that a deal with Unite was “‘within sight”.

He added that no settlement could be reached until the local election next week – but vowed to clear up the mess once and for all “as a matter of absolute priority”.

“Only Labour can end this dispute,” he warned.

The strike officially began in March last year, following a dispute over role changes and pay cuts. But recycling collections stopped even earlier, in January.

Unite, the union representing the refuse workers, claimed that council plans would result in over 150 employees seeing £8000 cuts to their salaries.



Local authorities argued the reforms would only affect a handful of workers.

The new deal, which Unite recently let slip, will include compensation of £16,000 to workers, an unprecedented offer which may well bring an end to the crisis.

But it may be too little too late for Birmingham residents, who have faced months of mid-summer stench and backyard bonfires due to irregular bin collections.

Earlier this week they marked 400 days since the strikes begun.

Anyone who has travelled across the city during the strike will notice that some areas have fared worse than others.



Elisha Marshall, 50, who lives on Carlton Road said: “Just look at this area and then go look at places like King’s Norton or King’s Heath – they look nothing like this.

“Luckily I am fit enough to take my recycling to the tip but even that’s a wind up.”

Elisha says you have to book a slot to visit the tip – it is not simply something you can do whenever it suits you.

Nisa Hasan, 55, who has lived on Carlton Road for decades said there was “no chance” she would vote for Labour.

To the side of her family home is a large area of wasteland, half the size of a football pitch, where her kids used to play cricket and football.



“It was a good open space. What has happened is beyond imagination.”

Now her walls are covered in crude graffiti and the play area for local kids has been littered with rubbish and turned into a make-shift car park.

“For months I had everything piled up at the side of the house – mattresses, garden waste, food waste, sofas.”

No one has been answering her desperate phone calls or emails about the mess – until now.

“Suddenly they say they are solving it because they need the votes,” she said.



Mona Abdelbari, 31, a mother of three, says she is “so sad” to wake up to piles of rotting rubbish every day.

“My children are so scared of the rats. We have had them in our house and got rid of a lot of furniture so it is easier to see them.”

Akhtar Zaman, 69, moved onto the road 57 years ago.

“All my life I have voted Labour,” he said. “This city has gone to the dogs and we need drastic action.”

Rodent infestations in the city are rife, with some residents reporting sightings of rats as large as cats.



Bin strikes are not exclusively to blame for the hideous state of some areas.

In these times of anarchy, fly-tippers have started taking advantage, such as the ten-foot-high heap of household waste dumped in March on a street residents dubbed a “Third World Slum”.

Birmingham Council have been contacted for comment.

News.title: What does UK’s ‘severe’ terror threat level actually mean? Security chiefs give verdict on ‘boiling point’ Britain
News.content:
ON ALERT What does UK’s ‘severe’ terror threat level actually mean? Security chiefs give verdict on ‘boiling point’ Britain

BRITAIN’S terror alert has been raised to the highest level in four years after a series of attacks on the streets on London.

Top officials announced the threat has been elevated from “substantial” to “severe” after two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green on Wednesday.





Fears of antisemitic attacks, activities of Iranian proxy groups and far-right actors operating on the streets of Britain are growing.

Ex-counter terror cop Chris Phillips warned the UK is at “boiling point”, while security expert Will Geddes said we are on a “war footing with terrorism“.

Both of them welcomed the decision by the government – and have broken down exactly what the new measures will mean.

They said Brits could see more armed officers at travel hubs and iconic sites across the country, and potentially even witness British troops used to bolster security at government sites.

The UK was last at its highest possible terror alert while under siege from ISIS-inspired thugs in 2017.

It was “critical” after the Tube bombing in Parsons Green that September.



Britain has previously used measures such as soldiers on the streets in “Operation Temperer” and SAS commandos from the “Blue Thunder” unit responding to terror attacks.

The UK-wide alert was last at the second tier “severe” level – as it is now – in November 2021 after a bomb explosion outside a hospital in Liverpool on Remembrance Sunday.

The Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre, which is based in MI5 but makes independent assessments, lowered the level back to “substantial” in February 2022.

Yesterday marked the first time the threat level has increased since then.

The official wording is that it is “highly likely” there could be an attack on British soil.



But what does that mean for the average Brit and how will it affect us?

Mr Phillips, the UK’s former counter-terrorism chief, explained officials have effectively judged how close Britain is to a terrorist strike.

The decision to raise the level is made by a combination of intelligence agencies across the country, including the army, navy, MI5, MI6 and cops.



Chris, a retired cop of 30 years service, told The Sun members of the public can expect to see more armed officers at transport hubs and busier areas.

He told us: “Generally it’s more about a little bit more overt policing.

“So firearms, you’ll probably see firearms officers at train stations, which you wouldn’t normally. You’ll see a slightly higher visibility patrols.

“This is effectively to tell iconic sites, who are more likely to be targeted by terrorists than others, that they need to step up their security.

“They may want to increase the number of high visibility guards outside and around the site as well.”



“You could say the Tower of London, all these sort of places, right across the country… even big shopping centres, stadiums, things like that.

“These sites should have a separate plan for when the terrorist threat goes up.”

Meanwhile, Mr Geddes – a private security specialist – said the “overt policing” strategy is designed to work as both a visual deterrent and reassurance for the public.

He explained there will be more work and surveillance going on behind the scenes for counter-terror cops and MI5 officials.

Will also spoke of an increased responsibility on the general public to remain vigilant and alert to suspicious behaviour.



Speaking to The Sun, he added: “It’s important for the general public to understand that threat levels are really more indicative.

“They’re amplified to basically say to the general public, you need to be a little bit more situationally aware. More aware of who’s around you…

“If you see an unattended bag, don’t just disregard it because the threat level is substantial… please report it. Be on your guard.

“Call the counter-terrorism hotline, if you call them, you never know. That small contribution could fit into a bigger puzzle or into a bigger picture.

“When you’re going with your family for a day out just be prepared a little bit more.”



Met Commissioner Mark Rowley, who was heckled with calls to resign after the double stabbing in North London, spoke about the terror alert today.

He reassured the public they should not “immediately change their behaviours”, but urged them to “be more alert”.

When asked if the decision had been made in the wake of the Golders Green attack, Chris instead pointed to the conflicts in Iran and Gaza.

He said: “No, I think it’s more about what’s happening in Iran and Gaza.

“It’s a boiling pot in that we’ve got a lot of people given the ability to talk about it through social media and stir themselves up.”



In the past, the Government has been forced to take more serious measures to combat terror across the UK.

Operation Temperer was activated by then-PM Theresa May in the wake of the Parsons Green Tube attack in September 2017.

Security chiefs drew up plans following a series of jihadi attacks in the Paris area in January 2015, including the Charlie Hebdo massacre.

Up to 5,100 troops would be used for “large-scale military support” in the wake of multiple attacks on British soil.

Soldiers would be deployed to guard key sites in major UK cities “to augment armed police officers engaged in protective security duties”.



And, in June 2017, members of an elite SAS unit were flown into London Bridge to help track down terrorists.

The move was made after a van was deliberately driven into pedestrians and then crashed on Borough High Street.

Attackers then ran to the nearby Borough Market area and began a horrifying rampage, stabbing people in and around restaurants and pubs.

The 70-strong squad, dubbed Blue Thunder – named for the unmarked helicopter they use for operations – were flown in from their Hereford HQ.

And Mr Geddes reckons the Government could consider bringing in troops in the coming weeks or months.



He said: “The government is going to be hugely resistant to it, but we may need to see those numbers buffering with uniformed military personnel.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Very possibly. I don’t see any harm. Why not? I think, you know, we are on a war footing with terrorism, moving us up to severe.

“We’re not a critical, but, you know, far, far rather, we put ourselves in a position where we’re minimizing the chances of moving to critical.”

News.title: Four teen boys, 13 to 16, arrested after man, 34, stabbed in the stomach outside McDonald’s
News.content:
KNIFE ATTACK Four teen boys, 13 to 16, arrested after man, 34, stabbed in the stomach outside McDonald’s

FOUR teenagers have been arrested after a 34-year-old man was stabbed in the stomach outside a McDonald’s.

Coppers were called to Briggate, Leeds, following reports of an altercation at 9.08pm on April 28.



The police have arrested four teenage boys, aged 13 to 16, at the scene of the assault.



The victim was rushed to hospital for his stab injury to the stomach, which was deemed non-life threatening.

West Yorkshire Police arrested four boys at the scene outside the McDonald’s on the corner of Briggate and Boar Lane.

The teenagers have since been released on bail while the police continue with its enquiries.

News.title: Ex-JPMorgan staffer accused of ‘fabricating’ sex slave claims against exec ‘asked chatbot for legal advice about rape’
News.content:
THE ex-JPMorgan staffer accused of making up sex slave claims against a top female exec allegedly asked a chatbot for legal advice on rape, reports claim.

Chirayu Rana, 35, has claimed in a bombshell lawsuit that high-ranking boss Lorna Hajdini, 37, sexually assaulted, racially abused and drugged him.





On legal-advice platform AskALawyerOnCall.com, an account, who is alleged to be Rana, asks questions about a suspected rape, the New York Post reported.

The exchange occurred in July, about 10 months ago, according to the website.

An account reportedly used by Rana – who initially filed his case under a John Doe pseudonym – began a chat with: “I was raped, secually assulted [sic], harassed, and forced to do drugs by my former boss at Morgan Stanley.”

He allegedly continued: “I was then retaliated against for seeking to move groups internally at the firm.



“HR conducted an ‘investigation’ but they ultimately made me signed [sic] a Separation Agreement.”

The user later called his alleged harasser as a “he” during two exchanges.



The site did not redact the customer’s name, saying: “Askalawyeroncall.com is a public forum and questions and responses are not private or confidential or protected by the attorney-client privilege.”

The customer reportedly identified himself as Rana and was asked by the bot if his “separation agreement’’ over the incident at the time included any clauses about waiving his rights to pursue legal action or discuss the matter publicly.

The user replied: “Yes but I was forced to sign under duress.”



The account added he had “AMPLE evidence” of his suffering.

Rana, who joined JPMorgan’s leveraged finance team in spring 2024, made an internal complaint against Hajdini in May 2025.

But the company eventually found no evidence of wrongdoing.

Rana was reportedly put in touch with a chatbot to a purported lawyer with the username Joycelaw.

They claimed to be an expert in a range of legal topics including business and employment law.



During the reported exchange, the user, allegedly Rana, identified his abuser as a man.

Rana’s headline-grabbing lawsuit has been withdrawn for “corrections” since it was filed earlier this week.

The account also said: “I was sexually assaulted and harassed by my former boss, and he even forced me to do drugs.

Rana is alleged to have started the conversation with the so-called lawyer, a transcript shows.

He allegedly wrote: “It’s been really hard to deal with. It’s been a tough time for me.



“I signed it because I was scared and felt I had no choice. He said he would ruin my career if I didn’t comply.

“After I signed, he started spreading lies about me, claiming I made everything up. It was disheartening because most people at work didn’t know the truth.

“I’ve been struggling mentally since then. It was a terrible experience, and I left under awful circumstances.

“He told everyone a false narrative about me, which made it even harder.”

The lawyer then appears to reference the alleged sexual assault cases, but says that they took place years before Rana joined the firm.



Joycelaw wrote: “Since this happened in 2020, you might still have options. Have you considered filing a workers’ compensation claim?”

Rana allegedly wrote back: “I didn’t think about that. I just feel stuck because I signed that waiver.

“Everyone seems to refuse to help me because of it.

He also allegedly claimed he lost a separate job because his alleged abuser “breached the NDA and told my new employer about what happened”.

Rana – who quit his last job at Bregal Sagemount on April 2, three weeks before his lawsuit against Hajdini – expressed intrigue at the idea of taking real legal action, the transcript reportedly shows.



He reportedly asks: “Do you think I actually have a valid claim?

“Do you know anyone who might take my case?”

JPMorgan, who were also co-accused in the suit of not preventing the alleged abuse, have confirmed that Rana had delivered a written complaint in May 2024.

He told the HR team detailing what he described as race and gender-based discrimination.

Rana then tried to negotiate a payoff with JPMorgan that ran into the “millions” which would have seen him leave the company and not take the claims to court, sources said.



The major US financial firm did not accept and instead launched an internal investigation where they found no evidence of wrongdoing from Hajdini.

Despite this, Rana’s attorney, Daniel J. Kaiser, has vowed to pursue his client’s claims after saying the banker is a victim of “horrific sexual abuse”.

He added: “As to Ms. Hajdini’s predictable denials, I look forward to discovery and, in particular, her deposition.

“The abuse occurred and we will prove it.”

Rana’s suit also alleges Hajdini used her position of power to threaten his job and withhold his yearly bonus to try and force him into nonconsensual sexual acts.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Hajdini vehemently denies all the claims with sources now claiming she didn’t even have the power to heavily influence his career.

News.title: Elon Musk set for massive £117BILLION pay day from Tesla – but here’s why he won’t see any of it
News.content:
ELON Musk is set for a massive £117billion pay day from Tesla – but will not be able to pocket any of it.

The staggering figure is part of a huge pay deal agreed between the firm and its billionaire boss last year.





Musk’s compensation figures were disclosed in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Thursday.

But the tech giant will only receive the cash if he manages to deliver ambitious milestones.

This includes raising the electric car company’s market value to £6.3trillion.

But analysts say he has a long way to go before he sees the monster cheque.

Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell, told the BBC: “Elon Musk isn’t actually going to pocket £117billion.”

None of the milestones set out in the pay deal approved last year were achieved in 2025, she added.

The deal approved a total £760billion sum.

It came after Musk threatened to quit Tesla and take his artificial intelligence plans to another business in his tech empire.



Musk is already the world’s richest man with a net worth estimated between $651billion and $788billion.

His firm SpaceX is also poised to become one of the most valuable publicly traded companies in the world.

The rocket-maker is gearing up for an initial public offering (IPO), which would allow its shares to be traded on the stock market.

The tech mogul has also been fighting a court battle over the direction taken by a rival firm – OpenAI – which he founded with current owner Sam Altman in 2015.

Musk has claimed that Altman and fellow executive Greg Brockman “stole a charity” when they pursued profit-generating initiatives that he felt contradicted the company’s founding mission.



Throughout the court hearing, Musk had numerous touchy interactions with lawyers for OpenAI and the judge.

Calling himself a fool for investing in OpenAI

Musk’s lawsuit claims the artificial intelligence giant allegedly prioritised profit despite promising to keep the company a nonprofit dedicated to benefiting humanity.

“I was a fool who provided them free funding to create a startup,” Musk said on the witness stand in a California courtroom, per Wall Street Journal.

“I gave them $38 million of essentially free funding to create what would become an $800 billion company.”



Musk contributed millions of dollars to the company, now valued at $852billion, between December 2015 and May 2017.

News.title: British boxer forced to pull out of fight after security use TEAR GAS on fans
News.content:
British boxer forced to pull out of fight after security use TEAR GAS on fans

Joe Laws was preparing to fight Elvis Ahorga in Lagos, Nigeria when the arena became filled with tear gas, as security desperately tried to control fans who were trying to enter the arena without tickets

View 2 Images The referee covered himself as the tear gas spread (Image: DAZN)

A British boxer was forced to pull out of his fight in Nigeria on Friday night after security used TEAR GAS on fans. Joe Laws had been due to face Ghana's Elvis Ahorga in Lagos, but the bout was cancelled after chaos ensued.

‌



Fans without tickets had attempted to force their way into the arena to watch the event which was headlined by a fight between two influencers, Portable and Carter Efe. Security used tear gas in order to get control of the situation and it spread around the venue.

‌



At the time, Laws was warming up away from the ring while Basit Adebayo was facing Loren Japhet on the undercard. The gas affected Laws' eyesight, as he explained in a Facebook post on Saturday morning.

‌



"Came as a honey badger left with sore eyes," the 31-year-old wrote. "Video posting today explaining." Laws labelled Ahorga and his team 'clowns' and said that he was: "Foaming."

Footage of the incident quickly went viral on social media. Women's heavyweight world champion Claressa Shields was among those to react, posting: "Wow this is pretty insane."

Another said on X: "This is really unfortunate. Hope all fighters, officials, and fans are safe." A third wrote: "What a fiasco."

Despite Laws and Ahorga's bout not going ahead, the boxing did eventually resume later in the night. Carter Efe beat Portable - a rapper by trade - following a unanimous decision. All three of the judges scored the fight 30-27 in favour of comedian Carter Efe.

Laws, who hails from Benwell, Newcastle, has been involved in 19 professional fights since he made his debut in 2018. His record stands at 15 wins and four losses.

‌



View 2 Images Joe Laws made his professional debut in 2018 (Image: Charlotte Tattersall/Getty Images)

In October 2024, Laws tragically lost his older brother, Jason, after he was killed alongside seven-year-old Archie York in an explosion which destroyed several homes in Benwell. Joe recalled during a subsequent interview with ITV Tyne Tees: "Every fight he would always just turn up - out of the blue.

"I love him to bits and he'll be a great miss. And it's true - life isn't fair sometimes. What can I do? Sit in the corner and cry? What's that going to solve? I've got kids that look up to me - I've got fantastic friends and fantastic family so the show will go on. The show must go on. I've got to stay strong and finish the mission I started years ago."

News.title: Mum of three loses 10 stone and is 'inundated' with messages - 'it's changed my life'
News.content:
Mum of three loses 10 stone and is 'inundated' with messages - 'it's changed my life'

Natalie Strange was a size 22 at her heaviest and was spending £250 a month on takeaways before transforming her life

View 4 Images Natalie before she lost a dramatic amount of weight (Image: Jam Press/Natalie Strange)

A mother of three has lost 10 stone and claims she's 'rediscovered herself'. Natalie Strange, 37, dropped 10 stone with assistance from "skinny" jabs. Natalie, from Norwich, describes Mounjaro as a "saving grace" in reclaiming her life and recovering the self-assurance she believed had vanished for good.

‌



As a stay-at-home mother of three, Natalie became a "shell" of who she once was, turning to food – spending £250 monthly on her takeaway "addiction". This caused her weight to soar to 19 stone, reaching a UK dress size 22 at her largest.

‌



"I had lost my self-worth and felt like I no longer had a purpose," she said. "After having kids, I lost my confidence and just ended up going with the flow.

‌



View 4 Images Natalie Strange now (Image: Jam Press/Natalie Strange)

"Each day was monotonous and boring. I lost sight of who I was."

In March 2024, she opted to try the weight loss treatment, and was delighted to shed 10 stone, slimming down to a trim size 10. With her restored confidence, 'happy' Natalie recognised that – despite attempting couple's therapy – her 18-year relationship had broken down. She said: "I had always gone into marriage thinking I'd be with that person forever. For me, divorce was off the table.

‌



"So there's that element of feeling like I've failed. And I do have that doubt of ruining my kids' lives – though they love having two Christmases, two holidays; basically two of everything.

View 4 Images Natalie Strange now (Image: Jam Press/Natalie Strange)

"Sometimes, I do wonder if I made a rash decision, but then we spend time together and I realise that isn't the case at all." She has since returned to the dating scene. She said: "When I joined, at first, I had really low expectations of anybody being interested in a single mum-of-three.

‌



"But, without blowing my own horn, I was inundated with men that wanted to talk to me. It was a huge eye opener and such an ego boost.

"I've found myself again and that sense of adventure I was hungry for. The jabs have changed my life.

View 4 Images Natalie before taking the skinny jab (Image: Jam Press/Natalie Strange)

Article continues below

"I'd have never had the confidence and bravery to step out on my own without them. Using them has given me the validation I was searching for.

"Now, the world is a kinder place and I'm living the life I once dreamed of – happy and free."

News.title: Reform and Tories would prolong Birmingham bin strike warns Labour deputy leader
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Reform and Tories would prolong Birmingham bin strike warns Labour deputy leader

Labour deputy leader Lucy Powell MP welcomed the deal struck between Labour and Unite union, but warned both Reform and Tories could rip it up and prolong the crisis

View 2 Images A deal has been struck to end the strikes (Image: PA)

An end to the Birmingham bin strikes is on the ballot paper when voters go to the polls next week, the Labour deputy leader has claimed.

‌



Lucy Powell MP welcomed the deal struck between Labour and Unite union, but warned both Reform and Tories could rip it up and prolong the crisis.

‌



The Labour-controlled city council announced this week that a negotiated settlement to bring the bitter 476-day dispute to a close is "within sight". Around 400 workers have been taking part in strikes since January last year, and the tense stand-off has seen rubbish piled up across the city for months.

‌



Birmingham bin strike end close to as deal put forward to finally resolve crisis READ MORE :

View 2 Images Lucy Powell warned the Tories and Reform could rip up a deal to end the strikes (Image: THE LABOUR PARTY)

‌



Ms Powell, the MP for Manchester Central, said: “The bin dispute in Birmingham has caused a stink for local residents for too long. The deal on the table will help clean up the city and is in the best interests of workers and council tax payers. Labour was founded by working people who wanted fairness, better pay and conditions and stronger rights at work and Labour continues to fight for that today.

“After the Labour Leader John Cotton decided to change tack, and thanks to the engagement by Unite and Sharon Graham, a deal to finally end the strikes is on the table. It’s clear that Reform and the Tories want to take a different course which would prolong the dispute. If the residents of Birmingham want to end the strikes and support the deal that’s been struck between the Labour leadership and unite, then they need to give Labour a clear mandate at these local elections in Birmingham on Thursday.”

The dispute first began over council plans to remove Waste Recycling and Collection Officer (WRCO) roles. Unite said the move would lead to pay cuts of around £8,000 for hundreds of its members. In January a report by the council's director of finance Carol Culley said the strike action had cost the authority £33.4million.

Article continues below

Unite said the agreement would ensure workers get at least a two years 'cushion' from the impact of the job evaluation process. This had previously been six months. Striking agency workers with at least 12 months of employment will also be offered a route to permanent jobs. Onay Kasab, Unite national lead officer, said the offer, which has not yet been put to the union’s members, includes compensation of £16,000 for workers.

News.title: Inside evil bully's home with 'torture chamber' where he abused vulnerable women
News.content:
Inside evil bully's home with 'torture chamber' where he abused vulnerable women

Sadistic bully Vince Agar has been jailed for 19 years at Teesside Crown Court after turning his Middlesbrough flat into a 'fortress' complete with a 'torture chamber', trapdoor and telescope to control and brutalise drug-addicted vulnerable women.

View 9 Images Vince Agar was jailed this week (Image: Cleveland Police)

Disturbing images expose the lengths to which Middlesbrough torturer Vince Agar would go in his twisted attempt to dominate vulnerable women.

‌



Throughout proceedings at Teesside Crown Court, jurors were presented with photographs of Agar's Parliament Road "fortress", captured by officers around the period of his offending. They revealed additional doors he had fitted, weapons left on surfaces and surveillance gear he employed to watch over those trapped under his drug-dealing grip.

‌



They can now be published after Agar was eventually held accountable for the litany of brutality he subjected two women to. On Thursday, he received a 19-year prison sentence with Judge Richard Bennett branding him a "sadistic bully", who "revelled in holding power over some of the most vulnerable women in our society."

‌



Agar was raised in Middlesbrough and grafted on oil rigs and at ICI. He resided with his parents before settling down with his wife Mary on Fleetham Street.

View 9 Images Agar pictured in 2009, receiving the keys to his new bungalow (Image: The Gazette)

Throughout the trial, he couldn't remember when he wed Mary, but did acknowledge conducting an affair with a woman - another casualty of his violence. In the horrific assault for which he was imprisoned in 2001, he battered her with an iron bar, glass bottle, hammer and a wrench, hacked off half her hair and burned her with cigarettes and scissors.

‌



This victim looked on as Agar was sentenced on Thursday for offences which displayed "chilling" parallels to her own nightmare. Agar had informed Teesside Crown Court during his trial that when Mary uncovered his crack cocaine use, around the age of 51, he departed their home and relocated to Parliament Road. Agar operated his drugs enterprise from the first floor flat, dealing cocaine to those trapped by addiction, including numerous exploited women and girls.

Situated in the heart of Newport's red light district, the neighbourhood at that time was ravaged by widespread drug use, violent crime and assaults on sex workers. Marilyn Surtees, who operated a drop-in centre for exploited women and girls at the time, previously told Teesside Live : "I remember there were a lot of rapes and girls being beaten up, lots of violence.

View 9 Images His flat looked out on to Union Street (Image: TeessideLive)

‌



"There was a lot of naming and shaming of the kerb crawlers but I don't think there were many arrests for violence. The girls either didn't report it or they weren't taken seriously."

Agar's first floor flat stood on the corner of Parliament Road and Longford Street. During the period of his offending, he maintained a pair of binoculars, a telescope and a tripod positioned by the window which overlooked Union Street directly.

This was employed, the prosecution stated, to monitor, and maintain control over, those whose drug addiction he exploited. Both Agar's victims were drug addicts. One was a sex worker who purchased her drugs from Agar. The other sold drugs on Agar's behalf. She told the court that Agar supplied her with free drugs and she would go out "grafting" for him while Agar spent time with his mistress. When she stole from him, Agar unleashed his twisted retribution.

‌



9 View 9 Images Agar had three extra doors installed in his flat, including one behind the front door (Image: CPS) 9 View 9 Images The front door and the extra door fitted behind it (Image: CPS)

Left defenceless by drugs, the woman was tied up with rope before Agar subjected her to hours of savage beating, initially wielding a metal hoover pole until it broke. He pressed heated knives against her arms, threatened to crush her fingers with a wrench, and made calls to an unidentified person in her presence, telling them to come and dispose of her body.

‌



In the second harrowing assault, he held her captive for three days. He once again used knives, along with sticks, buckles and belts. He heated his crack pipe and deliberately burned her on the upper arm, and branded her on her back, possibly with an iron.

Both ordeals left permanent scarring. At sentencing, Judge Richard Bennett told Agar the attacks were "on any view, sadistic and amounted to the torture of her."

View 9 Images Inside Agar's flat showing knives and drugs paraphernalia (Image: Cleveland Police)

‌



During the trial, jurors heard she had discovered a "torture chamber" within the flat, which housed an "old fashioned wooden chair" fitted with brown leather straps for the ankles and wrists. The second of Agar's terrified victims revealed that Agar threatened to shoot her after she witnessed a "scared" girl, believed to be a sex worker, bound to a radiator. The court was told, through her witness statement, how she has carried guilt and anguish for failing to report the incident to police. The judge informed Agar: "Such was your reputation at the time, she was too terrified to tell anyone apart from her boyfriend, and she discouraged her boyfriend from intervening, for fear of what you may do."

Doors fitted to 'keep women against their will'

The jury was additionally presented with photographs of supplementary doors Agar had fitted in his flat, including one positioned behind the front entrance and a "trapdoor" at the top of the stairs. Prosecutor Ms Brown had suggested the additional doors formed part of an "elaborate security arrangement" to administer his own brand of justice.

View 9 Images Agar was addicted to crack cocaine and sold it (Image: Cleveland Police)

‌



She said: "You didn't want people coming in because of your drug-dealing and because you were being violent to women in there and keeping them against their will?" In his sentencing remarks, Judge Bennett informed Agar: "Your flat was like a fortress.

"You had installed a number of doors to the interior to prevent access. They also prevented escape.

"These were classic security measures of a drug dealer designed to prevent the police getting into your flat before you could dispose of drugs. That anti-police security also created a barrier which prevented [victim] from escaping." It was put to the court that Agar flogged his drugs almost entirely to sex workers at the time. Ms Brown challenged him in court: "You didn't care about these girls at all did you? Did it ever bother you what they were doing to afford the drugs they were using?

‌



View 9 Images Agar had a tripod, telescope and binoculars at the window of his front room (Image: Cleveland Police)

"Did you ever worry about your customers' safety. Did you like the fact these girls were indebted to you? Did you like that they were reliant on you? Did you like the power over them?"

Agar featured in the Evening Gazette when he relocated to a new housing scheme in Middlesbrough town centre. Mary and Vince became the first shared owners to settle into the £9million St Paul's development in Newport through Erimus Housing's shared ownership scheme.

Article continues below

View 9 Images Spying equipment at the flat (Image: Cleveland Police)

Several years afterwards he relocated to Thailand, "met a lady, she had a baby, I brought the baby up, so I stayed in Thailand". As officers compiled evidence, Agar attempted to evade justice, declining to return of his own accord.

An extradition procedure was initiated and he was transported back to Middlesbrough to answer for his historical offences. During the entire legal proceedings, Agar persisted in inflicting trauma on his victims - his denials meaning they had to relive their ordeals in a trial spanning more than three weeks. The jury was not fooled by his deceit, and in March he was found guilty of six out of the eight charges brought against him. As Judge Bennett declared when sentencing Agar to 19 years behind bars: "You got away with committing these serious offences for 25 years and this has now caught up on you."

News.title: Massive UK water park reopens this Bank Holiday with huge new 39ft slide
News.content:
Massive UK water park reopens this Bank Holiday with huge new 39ft slide

It is reopening for the summer season this Bank Holiday weekend - and it's got a brand new 39ft X Tower mega slide for thrill-seekers

View 3 Images (Image: Jam Press/Cliff Lakes)

A major UK water park is set to reopen just in time for the Bank Holiday weekend – and adventure seekers have an enormous new attraction awaiting them. The renowned Aqualand inflatable water park returns for the summer season, unveiling a brand-new mega slide designed for adrenaline enthusiasts.

‌



Reaching an impressive 12m (39ft) in height, the new "X Tower" offers high-speed descents, racing lanes and a pulse-racing experience not suited to the faint of heart. While the main park reopens this week, visitors will need to wait slightly longer before attempting the imposing new feature.

‌



View 3 Images (Image: Jam Press/Cliff Lakes)

‌



Aqualand, located at Cliff Lakes in Tamworth, near Birmingham, will reopen on Saturday (2 May), with the X Tower scheduled to launch on Saturday (23 May), perfectly timed for the second Bank Holiday weekend and school half-term. The X Tower boasts six slides, incorporating dual racing lanes and precipitous drop sections engineered for extra thrills.

The new attraction forms part of a broader expansion at the venue, with another feature – the "Wibit Wave" – also debuting this summer. The wave-style slide extends 15 metres and stands five metres high, providing a more lighthearted yet still dynamic ride.

Article continues below

View 3 Images The slide is 39 foot tall (Image: Jam Press/Cliff Lakes)

The water park already hosts eight inflatable obstacle courses that visitors can navigate during 80-minute sessions. Participants must be aged six or above and at least 1.10 metres tall to join in, while younger children require adult supervision. Visitors must also be confident swimmers and capable of completing 25 metres unaided before taking to the water.

The entry price covers a wetsuit and buoyancy aid, with all guests obliged to wear the appropriate safety gear throughout their session, bosses say. Anyone keen to take on the X Tower will need to pay an extra £5 on top of the standard admission price.

News.title: LUCY POWELL: 'Labour must show more strongly we are here for you and your family'
News.content:
LUCY POWELL: 'Labour must show more strongly we are here for you and your family'

'Labour has always been, and will always be, on the side of ordinary people, unafraid to take on those who want to stop us', Labour Deputy Leader Lucy Powell writes

View 2 Images Lucy Powell said Labour had been too quiet in how it took on power and vested interests (Image: PP.)

BP profits more than doubling as a result of the Iran war makes us all cross. It’s why Labour was right to tax windfall energy profits. Despite pressure from some, we continue to do so.

‌



But this illustrates something bigger. Each time an economic crisis comes along some profit from, and exploit, the situation while everyone else pays the price. In the global financial crisis in 2008, we bailed out the banks but ordinary people paid with austerity.

‌



During Covid, a few benefited from the VIP fast lane or de-frauded the loan scheme, while the rest saw living standards fall. And just like the last energy price shock, we are seeing excess profits for some companies.

‌



Keir Starmer warns impact of Middle East conflict on UK could be as severe as Covid READ MORE :

View 2 Images Lucy Powell welcomed an end to the Birmingham bin strikes

Because rising costs - food, energy, housing - affects those on modest incomes or fixed incomes the most - it’s a bigger proportion of earnings. This time, we have a Labour government, and things have to be different. Indeed, tackling the unequal weathering of these storms and fundamentally rewiring the economy so it works for you, is what this Labour Government is all about. Perhaps too quietly, we have been taking on those with power and vested interests to rip up the status quo.

This is not our war. Keir Starmer was absolutely right to keep us out of it. But we have to deal with its consequences. Another energy price shock shows that establishing GB Energy and our sprint to clean, homegrown power, is the only route to protecting us in future. Now we need to race ahead.

‌



It’s also why protecting workers and giving the lowest paid a pay rise - in paypackets this week - is crucial to building a fairer economy. And from last Friday Labour’s Renter’s Rights Act will stabilise rents, stop rent hikes and end bidding wars. Vested interests told us we couldn’t do any of these things but we have.

It’s far from job done. We need to go further and faster. I know people are frustrated. They’re disillusioned. I hear that. We must show more strongly we are here for you and your family, especially in the more difficult times. We are.

Be under no illusion, Nigel Farage and Reform are not friends of working people. They want to scrap that windfall energy tax I was talking about. They believe in an insurance system for the NHS - essentially an NHS that you pay for (if you can afford it). In the councils they control, they’ve put up taxes and cut services. Don’t forget, Reform and the Tories wanted us to blindly follow Trump into this war in the first place. While we’re on other political parties, the Greens and Zack Polanski have shown their true colours this week, criticising the police for how they apprehended the Golders Green attacker.

‌



No one gets everything right, but with many people going to the polls this Thursday to elect their local representatives, it is Labour that has always been, and will always be, on the side of ordinary people, unafraid to take on those who want to stop us.

'Welcome end to Birmingham bin strikes'

I go to Birmingham often and I know what a huge issue the bin strikes and lack of recycling has been for residents, as it has been for bin workers too. So, I strongly welcome the Labour Leader of Birmingham Council John Cotton’s offer to workers to end them, and the positive reaction from Sharon Graham of Unite the Union.

Equal Pay and relations with the workforce have been a thorny and complex issue for a while, so this huge development is welcome news. I know how hard the Labour leadership and the union have worked to find a resolution. This deal is in the interests of the city, its workers, its residents, and its future. Well done all!

Article continues below

'Good luck those taking exams'

May 7th is a big day in my house. No, not the local elections (although they’re big too), it’s my daughter's first GCSE exam. She’s got 26 exams in total - which is too many in my view. GCSE’s are much tougher than in my day. Our young people work really hard and put themselves under a lot of pressure - mine do anyway! Good luck to all those taking big exams.

'Here's to Arsenal bottling it'

I try not to talk about football with Keir Starmer - he’s famously a big Arsenal fan, and I’m a big Manchester City fan. Yet again, these final few weeks in the title race are going down to the wire. It’s way too tense to discuss! Here’s to Arsenal bottling it again (sorry boss!)

News.title: General Strike paralysed UK in fight for living wage while Tories got vindictive revenge
News.content:
General Strike paralysed UK in fight for living wage while Tories got vindictive revenge

Nearly two million workers joined Britain's first – and only – General Strike, which began at midnight on 3 May 1926, in support of starving miners and their families

View 5 Images Tottenham North London scene during the General Strike of 1926 (Image: Daily Mirror)

At midnight on 3 May 1926, nearly two million workers joined Britain's first – and only – General Strike. Their walkout in support of starving miners and their families was the greatest act of working class solidarity in history. But it wasn't enough. The nationwide stoppage, called by the TUC General Council, virtually paralysed the nation as railwaymen, transport workers and printers heeded the call for sympathetic action. Workers walked off the job from John O'Groats to Land's End, in an exhilarating show of unity that surprised even the strike leaders.

‌



But after only nine days, accused by the Tory government of fomenting a Communist revolution, TUC chiefs lost their nerve and called off the strike, leaving the miners to fight on alone until humiliating defeat six months later. 1926, a searing memory in the hearts and minds of trade unionists, is being commemorated across the country – most poignantly today in Barnsley, [2 May] where former miners demonstrate, with their union banners held proudly aloft.

‌



NINE DAYS THAT SHOOK BRITAIN Inside the General Strike 100 years on as establishment 'bullied' workers READ MORE :

They have more reason than anyone to remember, because their year-long Great Strike for Jobs of 1984/5 was a virtual replay of 1926, on a smaller but no less devastating, scale. That, too, resulted in vindictive Tory revenge. It all began when coal owners, determined to sustain profits under pressure from international competition, demanded a cut in colliers’ wages from £6 to a pittance of less than £3 a week. Even King George V said: “Try living on their wages before you judge them.”

‌



View 5 Images Engineering workers at Fort Dunlop in Birmingham today voted to continue strike action, now in it’s fifth week, Thursday 4th June 1970. (Image: Mirrorpix)

But Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin had already decided on confrontation with the Miners' Federation, setting up a paramilitary Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies, mobilising the army, police and volunteer strike-breakers. Historian AJP Taylor recorded: “The Cabinet wanted a strike.” And they got one, just like Thatcher in 1984.

The TUC general council, set up only the year before, lacked confidence and had no control over the walkout. Local committees sprang up to co-ordinate picketing, food and distribution of an official strike paper, the British Worker, which reported “workers calm and steady.”

‌



The strike was originally called in several key sectors - the railways, buses and trams, newspapers, docks, and iron and steel trades. But such was the enthusiasm that, for example in the West Midlands, there was trouble keeping men in work who were not involved. Scunthorpe was “like a town of the dead from the industrial point of view.”

The government set up an official newspaper, The British Gazette, edited by Winston Churchill, priced one penny. Its first headline on 5 May, blustered ‘The First Day of the Great Strike: Not So Complete as Hoped by Its Promoters.’ It reported a “mushroom town of ordered activity in Hyde Park” created to handle milk supplies to the capital.

View 5 Images General Strike Scene May 1926: London Street scene as people rush to catch buses (Image: Daily Mirror)

‌



Churchill opined: “This is a conflict between union leaders and Parliament. And that conflict can only end, and must only end, in the unmistakable victory of Parliament. This victory His Majesty's Government is definitely resolved to secure.” The TUC general council, clearly taken aback by their own runaway success, feared deliberate misrepresentation of precisely this sort. “This is an industrial dispute,” they insisted. “There is no constitutional crisis. The sole aim of the strike is to secure for the miners a decent standard of life.”

Considering the vast numbers of men on strike in so many towns and cities, and the passions aroused by such unprecedented action, 1926 was largely peaceful. But more than 5,000 arrests for violence and sedition were recorded, and some rioting took place in the industrial North of England and Scotland. Parliament's sole Communist MP, Shapurji Saklatvala, was arrested for calling on “the Army boys” not to fight strikers.

There were ugly scenes in the London docks on 8 May, when unarmed soldiers broke the picket line and escorted food lorries to Hyde Park. And when tram services restarted in Plymouth, crowds attacked vehicles and smashed windows. That same day, the British Worker reported “50,000 out and not one case of blacklegging” at Woolwich, with “the great Arsenal and Dockyard like an industrial museum, no sound of a hammer breaks the stillness throughout the hundreds of shops and not a wheel turning.”

‌



View 5 Images General Strike Scene May 1926: Scene in Hyde park as the temporary milk depot is set up (Image: Daily Mirror)

The worst, and potentially most disastrous, incident took place on 10 May, when striking miners derailed the Flying Scotsman at Cramlington, just north of Newcastle. An eight-man gang, believing the train carried coal, sabotaged the rails, causing the engine and several coaches of the southbound express to come off the track and overturn. The train was slowing down, and miraculously, only one of the 281 passengers suffered a minor foot injury. The eight men were jailed for up to eight years.

As the strike went into its second week, the government claimed that supplies were improving everywhere, with more trains running and record numbers of volunteer “specials” signing up, especially in London. Strike editions of Right-wing national newspapers carried stories of scarf-waving university students driving trains, but they were never much more than propaganda photo-shoots. One passenger thought it all “very jolly” watching an immaculate youth in plus-fours with a green flag telling his driver: “I say, you might go !”

‌



The end, when it came with indecent haste, was anything but jolly. As later happened in 1984, the High Court ruled the dispute unlawful and made the unions liable for unlimited damages. On 12 May the TUC called off the strike, with no commitment for employers to take back any dismissed men, and no deal for the miners.

View 5 Images The Imperial Typewriters strike 5th May 1974 saw hundreds of mainly Asian workers protest for nearly three months. (Image: Mirrorpix)

The government trumpeted “surrender in Downing Street,” and fast-tracked new laws banning general or sympathy strikes and mass picketing. The miners, led by legendary leader A.J.Cook, with his slogan “Not a penny off the pay, not a minute on the day!” fought on, gradually returning to work on lower wages, until the last were starved back in late November. The blame game that began then has never really ended. The miners accused the TUC of betrayal, the TUC thought it “best to avoid useless sacrifice” because the miners had determined on a fight to the finish.

Article continues below

In 1985, Arthur Scargill, the reincarnation of A.J.Cook, criticised the TUC for failing to mobilise the whole labour movement in support of his members. They, too, went down to defeat and the subsequent destruction of their union and the coal industry. One thing is indisputable: 1926 was - to use the words of their most ruthless opponent at the time - “the miners' finest hour.'

Sir Keir Starmer has backed a ban on some pro-Palestine protests as part of a crackdown on antisemitism in the wake of the Golders Green terror attack.

The prime minister suggested there were “instances” where it was appropriate to prevent such marches happening on UK streets - as they have done in France - and said he would fight “with every breath I have” for a diverse and tolerant Britain.

He also issued a stark challenge to those who take part in the protests, saying if they hear chants of ‘globalise the Intifada’ - “you do have to stop and ask yourself, why am I not calling this out?”

But the government’s independent adviser on antisemitism told The Independent it would be “unconscionable” to outlaw peaceful pro-Palestine protests.

open image in gallery Prime minister Sir Keir Starmer and Metropolitan Police commissioner Sir Mark Rowley meet first responders from Shomrim North West London during a visit to Golders Green (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire )

Lord Mann said: “There are multiple small anti-Israel (or similar) protests every week. Usually involving a tiny number of people.

“If they are not calling for violence… then it is unconscionable in a democracy that any such concept could be acted upon. The safety and security of the Jewish community requires effective strong leadership - not gestures.”

Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti added: “It’s perfectly reasonable for political leaders to urge sensitivity and restraint around protests in the wake of terrorist violence and the fear it breeds. But it is quite another thing to equate protest with violence or to clamp down on peaceful dissent even further.

“I urge the government to lead by example and demonstrate the balanced judgment they recommend to others.”

Sir Keir’s call came in an interview with the BBC’s Today programme, just days after he was heckled during a visit to Golders Green, where he was met by a group of protesters holding signs and chanting: "Keir Starmer, Jew Harmer".

Asked if he wanted a crackdown on the chants or to stop some protests altogether, he told the BBC: “I think certainly the first, and I think there are instances for the latter.”

He added: “I don't want to get involved in operational policing, but I think when you see, when you hear some of those chants, ‘globalise the Intifada’ the one that I would pick out, then clearly there should be tougher action in relation to that.”

open image in gallery Keir Starmer said he would fight ‘with every breath I have’ for a diverse and tolerant Britain. ( Getty )

He went on: “In relation to the repeated nature of the marches, many people in the Jewish community have said to me ‘it's the repeat nature, it's the cumulative effect’. Now I accept that, which is why we intend to deal with cumulative effects.”

He urged “some people protesting to just reflect on what the Jewish community is going through and the overall impact that this is having.”

The PM also called for a “whole of society response” saying that “too many people are not seeing antisemitism or they don't want to see it.”

Addressing those on the marches, but not involved in the chanting, he said: “If you are on a march or a protest where people are chanting ‘globalise the Intifada’ you do have to stop and ask yourself, why am I not calling this out?”

He added: “We all have to fight for this together because it is about the sort of country that we want to live in. I want to live in the Britain that I love, which is a decent, tolerant, live and let live, diverse Britain. But that is contested now in a way that it hasn't been contested in my lifetime.

“We have to fight for the Britain that we believe in with those values. That is who we are. That is what it is to be British. And I will fight for that with every breath I have.”

Lord Walney, the government’s former adviser on political violence, said: "The prime minister sounds committed and sincere but he’s not offering anything different - he needs to stop refusing the law changes that would genuinely reduce the harm being caused by these hate-infested marches."

But Your Party Chair Jenn Forbes said her party condemned “all attempts to link the safety of Jewish communities with restrictions on protests for Palestine”.

The Golders Green stabbings are the latest in a series of attacks on Jewish sites since the outbreak of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran, and have prompted accusations that the UK government has not done enough to tackle antisemitism.

On Friday, Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley called for 300 extra officers to tackle the growing pandemic of antisemitism in the UK.

He also said he was considering whether police powers should be used to limit two upcoming protests in London later in May – one a pro-Palestine march and the other a rally led by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson.

Britain’s terror threat has been raised to severe, meaning authorities believe an attack in the UK is “highly likely” in the next six months, after the stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green, London.

Explaining the move on Friday, MI5 said the UK has been experiencing a gradual increase in terrorist threats for some time, driven by a rise in both Islamist and extreme right-wing terror.

Animal welfare organisations have announced an agreement to purchase nearly 1,500 beagles from a Wisconsin dog breeding and research facility, which recently became the scene of a violent confrontation between activists and police. The incident earlier this month saw law enforcement use tear gas and pepper spray to repel campaigners attempting to breach the premises.

Big Dog Ranch Rescue and the Center for a Humane Economy confirmed a confidential deal with Ridglan Farms to acquire 1,500 of the approximately 2,000 beagles housed there, for an undisclosed sum. The fate of the remaining dogs at the facility remains uncertain. Ridglan Farms has not yet responded to requests for comment.

Lauree Simmons, president and founder of Big Dog Ranch Rescue, expressed her delight to The Associated Press, stating: "It's a very big win and I am ecstatic to have these dogs out and get them into loving homes." Ms Simmons declined to elaborate on the financial terms of the agreement, its duration, or the precise number of beagles still at Ridglan following the transaction.

The 1,500 beagles are scheduled for transport later this week from Ridglan to various partner agencies, as well as to Big Dog Ranch Rescue’s own facilities in Florida and Alabama. There, they will undergo medical examinations, microchipping, and vaccinations before being evaluated for adoption.

Ms Simmons highlighted the significant adjustment these animals face: "These dogs need to learn to walk on a leash. They need to learn to live in a home environment, be housebroken, spayed and neutered." She added that should an adoption not prove successful, the dogs are always welcome to return to Big Dog Ranch Rescue, which operates the largest cage-free, no-kill dog rescue in the US from its Loxahatchee, Florida, facility.

open image in gallery Animal rights activists protesting in the Wisconsin State Capitol show off wounds they say they suffered when they clashed with police two days earlier outside of a dog breeding and research facility, Monday, April 20, 2026, in Madison, Wis. (AP Photo/Scott Bauer) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Animal activists have been pushing for 10 years to have the dogs at Ridglan Farms adopted, not sold to other research facilities.

Simmons said her group was not involved in the recent protests that drew increased attention on Ridglan, but she credited activists with raising awareness about what was happening.

“What they did was put the message out," Simmons said of the activists. “What we did, we wanted to do legally and in the best way and for the best outcome of these dogs for the future.”

About 1,000 activists from across the country came to Ridglan Farms in rural Blue Mounds in an attempt on April 18 to take the beagles kept there about 25 miles (about 40 kilometers) southwest of the capital, Madison. They were met by police who repelled them with tear gas, rubber bullets and pepper spray. The Dane County Sheriff’s Department said 29 people were arrested and five face felony burglary charges.

open image in gallery Law enforcement in riot gear walk in a field after animal welfare activists attempted to gain entry to Ridglan Farms beagle breeding and research facility on Saturday, April 18, 2026, in Blue Mounds, Wis. (Owen Ziliak/Wisconsin State Journal via AP) ( Wisconsin State Journal )

Activists filed a federal lawsuit in Wisconsin last week alleging that police used unnecessary force to repel those trying to break into the facility and take the dogs. Ridglan has said those who tried to break in were a “violent mob” who launched “an assault on a federally licensed research facility."

In March, activists broke into Ridglan and left with 30 beagles. Sixty-three people were referred from the sheriff's department to the district attorney for potential charges related to that break in.

Ridglan Farms agreed in October to give up its state breeding license as of July 1 as part of a deal to avoid prosecution on felony animal mistreatment charges. Ridglan Farms has denied mistreating animals, but a special prosecutor determined that Ridglan Farms was performing eye procedures on the dogs that violated state veterinary standards.

Pope Leo XIV on Saturday encouraged some of the wealthiest U.S. Catholics to keep on giving to support his charitable works, in an audience that confirmed how the election of the first U.S.-born pope has invigorated American Catholics and their donations.

The Chicago-born Leo met with members of The Papal Foundation, a major funder of papal development projects in the developing world, in the Apostolic Palace at the end of their annual pilgrimage to Rome.

In his remarks, Leo thanked the foundation stewards for their generosity, which he said had allowed "countless people to experience in a concrete fashion the goodness and kindness of God in their own communities.”

He noted in particular the priests and nuns from poor countries who are able to study at Rome’s pontifical universities to earn advanced degrees thanks to scholarships funded by foundation’s grants, which combined over the past four decades have totaled more than $270 million.

While The Papal Foundation contributions to the Vatican remained strong during Pope Francis’ 12-year pontificate, other donations to the Holy See tanked during the global financial crisis, COVID-19 and other strains. Some U.S. Catholics also soured on donating to the Holy See following years of unrelenting stories of mismanagement, corruption and scandal, as well as Francis’ known criticism of American-style capitalism.

The election of Leo seems to have reinvigorated the U.S. church, especially the donor class. On Saturday The Papal Foundation announced that its members had approved more than $15 million in grants for 2026, a record in the foundation’s 38-year history.

The foundation also announced that 25 new families had joined it in the year since Leo’s election, in the strongest sign yet that the election of an American, English-speaking pope — and a math major with an eye to the Vatican's balance sheet — has been good news for church fundraising.

“The growth we’re seeing is incredibly encouraging, as it reflects a shared commitment to serve, to give, and to bring the church’s mission to life in meaningful ways across the globe,” David Savage, the foundation’s executive director, said in a statement.

The foundation was created by the late Cardinal John Krol of Philadelphia in 1988, as a way for wealthy U.S. Catholics to directly fund charitable initiatives of the pope.

To become a steward requires a $1 million gift to a fund that then helps support papal projects, such as building orphanages or monasteries. For 2026, for example, some of the approved projects include the construction or renovation of a safe school for marginalized tribal children in India, and professional technical training for vulnerable women in the Philippines.

The foundation currently has as its members all the U.S. cardinals, and is governed by a board of trustees made up of Catholic laypeople and bishops.

News.title: Lando Norris takes Miami GP sprint pole to deny Mercedes for first time in 2026
News.content:
McLaren’s world champion Lando Norris claimed pole for Saturday’s sprint race in Miami, denying Mercedes top spot for the first time in a competitive session this season.

Norris beat Mercedes’ championship leader Kimi Antonelli into second by a pretty handy margin, 0.222 seconds, as the top teams unveiled what they had been working on during Formula One’s enforced five-week break.

Norris’s team-mate Oscar Piastri will start third on Saturday morning with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fourth and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen fifth, just ahead of Mercedes’ title favourite George Russell. That is not a sentence anyone expected to write heading into the weekend.

Russell told Sky Sports F1 he was “surprised” by the extent of the progress made by Mercedes’ rivals over the break, particularly McLaren and Ferrari. “It’s pretty damn impressive,” he said.

“We knew they had probably closed the gap but all day they were quicker than us. From my side I’ve been struggling. Miami is not a track I love, especially in these hotter conditions. But it’s only sprint qualifying so let’s see what tomorrow brings. I’ve been quite surprised by the progress of the others. I’m not in a great starting position.”

McLaren Ferrari and Red Bull appear to have used the five-week gap profitably, arriving in Miami with a raft of upgrades and squeezing the gap at the top to Mercedes.

News.title: Mortgage approvals surge as buyers race to beat higher rates
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices rose unexpectedly last month despite the Iran war increasing the likelihood of higher interest rates this year.

Property values jumped by 0.4pc during April to £278,880, according to Nationwide.

Analysts had expected prices to fall by 0.3pc last month after consumer confidence was hit by the Iran war.

House prices were up 3pc compared to the same month last year, well ahead of forecasts for 2.2pc and up from 2.2pc in the 12 months to March.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said the figures were “somewhat surprising given that indicators of consumer confidence have weakened noticeably”.

He said: “Despite the uncertainty caused by developments in the Middle East and the subsequent rise in energy prices, the UK housing market has continued to regain momentum following the slowdown recorded around the turn of the year.”

House prices have risen despite money markets ramping up bets on the Bank of England raising interest rates this year to combat an expected rise in inflation.

On Thursday, the Bank kept rates at 3.75pc but warned inflation could rise above 6pc. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Shares rose in Asia, although most markets in the region were closed for May Day holidays.

Brent crude’s price rose 67 cents to $111.07 per barrel while US benchmark crude oil added 10 cents to $105.17 a barrel.

Prospects for a deal to cement a three-week ceasefire in the Middle East conflict remained clouded as Iran’s supreme leader said it will protect its nuclear and missile capabilities as a national asset.

The war’s shocks to oil supplies and prices are putting pressure on Donald Trump, who was floating a new plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passageway for oil and gas exports from the Middle East.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 gained 0.7pc to 59,678.31 as the Japanese yen gained against the US dollar.

On Wall Street stocks ended the day higher as investors digested a raft of economic data and the price of oil eased back from a four year high.

Figures released on Thursday showed that the US economy grew by 2pc in the first three months of 2026, while the nation’s jobless claims fell to their lowest level since 1969.

The economic data and strong corporate earnings caused shares to climb in New York.

The S&P 500 rose 1pc on Thursday and recorded a monthly gain of 10.4pc - its largest in more than five years.

The Nasdaq closed 0.9pc higher and rose 15.3pc during April. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.6pc in the last trading session of the month.
